NeuroGate · results

A small chip design that labels network packets

NeuroGate is a hardware design, written in SystemVerilog (a language for describing digital circuits), that reads network packets and labels each one as normal, a port scan (one machine probing many ports to find open ones) or a SYN flood (a burst of connection requests that are never finished, meant to overload a server; SYN, short for synchronize, is the first message of a connection). A tiny neural network with 8-bit integer weights makes the call from eight numbers about each packet and the recent traffic. This page collects the measured results.

Read this first. Every number on this page is either simulated (from a simulation run in this repository) or an estimate (from a synthesis or timing tool, with no place and route, the step that lays out and wires a real chip). Nothing ran on an FPGA (field-programmable gate array, a reprogrammable chip) or in silicon. All network traffic is synthetic, made by the project's own generator, so the accuracy here is not real-world accuracy. Each table and figure names the committed file its numbers come from.

Accuracy

How often the label is right, on packets the network never saw during training. The numbers come from the Python golden model, the bit-exact reference that the chip is tested against.

The int8 network (the arithmetic the chip uses) is right on 95.50% of 8,347 test packets. The floating-point network it was converted from scores 95.45%; the two give the same label on 99.90% of packets. Of the 9,000 test frames, 653 are dropped by the header readers as malformed or unsupported and are not counted here.

Precision and recall per class, int8 network, test split. Precision: of the packets given this label, the share that truly are this class. Recall: of the packets of this class, the share that got this label.

Confidence margin vs accuracy

With each label the chip reports a confidence: the gap between the two largest network outputs, scaled to 0-127. It is a margin, not a probability. Packets below a threshold are flagged as low confidence, so software can treat them with care. This chart shows whether a bigger margin really means a more reliable label.

Waveform from a real simulation

A timing diagram shows signals over time, as a logic analyser would. These two are drawn by the page script straight from the signal dump of a real simulation run; nothing is drawn by hand.

The run is the throughput test tb/test_neurogate_top_throughput.py (seed 12345, Icarus Verilog simulator, the whole chip at the source-code level): 14 generated frames are sent back to back on the network clock and the result output is always ready. Timing

Static timing analysis adds up gate delays along every path between flip-flops and checks that signals arrive in time for the next clock edge. Slack is the time to spare: positive means the check is met. The tool is OpenSTA with the Nangate45 typical library, ideal clocks and no wires (no place and route). Clock targets: network clock 6.4 ns (156.25 MHz), core clock 5 ns (200 MHz).

Worst slack per check, in nanoseconds
CheckNetwork clockCore clockResult
Setup, flip-flop to flip-flop+4.694+2.649met (estimate)
Hold, flip-flop to flip-flop+0.080+0.080met (estimate)
Setup, from input pins+4.814+2.810met (estimate)
Setup, to output pins+4.946+2.931met (estimate)
Clock crossing into this clock (limit 5.0 ns)+4.856+4.627met (estimate)
Reset release, recovery+6.261+4.861met (estimate)
Reset release, removal-0.108-0.108missed by 0.108 ns: not done, because there is no place-and-route step
  • Setup is met on both clocks (estimate). Real wires, clock-tree delay and other operating corners would reduce these margins.
  • Reset removal: the reset-release check at the asynchronous reset pins of the clock-crossing queue misses by 0.108 ns on both clocks. It is reported as not done, because there is no place-and-route step, which is where such a short path is normally padded with delay.
  • Pin budget is a guess: the design has no stated outside timing, so the constraints assume the logic outside the chip uses 20% of the clock period on each side.

synthesized (estimate) Source: synth/reports/sta.txt, synth/neurogate_top.sdc. Report label: “estimate (Nangate45 typical liberty, ideal clocks, no place and route)”

Throughput

How many packets per second the chip could label. This is a cycle count from simulation multiplied by the target clock, not a measured line rate.

Throughput test, whole chip, source-code level
MeasureValue
Core clocks per packet when packets are waiting179.0 (min 179, max 179, over 11 gaps)
Packets per second at 200 MHzabout 1,117,000
Delay of the first packet, last input beat to result187 core clocks (935 ns at 200 MHz)
Input side, network clocks per frame42.0 (mean frame 321 bytes)

The network core (one multiply-add unit doing all the work) is the bottleneck; the input side is faster. Whether the core really reaches 200 MHz is the timing estimate above, not this test.

Limitations

  • Synthetic data. All traffic comes from this repository's own generator. Accuracy here is not real-world accuracy.
  • Simulation only. No FPGA or silicon run. Throughput is a cycle count times the target clock.
  • Timing is a pre-layout estimate. Ideal clocks, no wires, one operating corner, a guessed pin budget, and one open reset-removal miss.
  • Confidence is a margin, not a probability.
  • Clock crossings were checked by a structural script and a written review, not by a commercial tool or a formal proof.

The full list is in the Limitations section of the README.

This page is generated by scripts/build_results_page.py from the committed result files named in each section. make results-check rebuilds it and fails if this file differs, so a number edited by hand is caught.
